blocks.label: A  ·  BIG IDEAS
items: 1. Time scale: Its four units, largest to smallest: → Eon, era, period, epoch.
2. Fossils: What kind of rock holds most of them? → Sedimentary rock: layers of sediment bury and preserve remains.
3. Dating: What method finds the age of very old rock? → Radiometric dating (uranium-lead, potassium-argon). Carbon-14 dates organic material younger than about 50,000 years.
4. CO₂: When it builds up in the air, what happens to temperatures? → They go up: Earth warms.
5. Ice: When ice sheets grow, what happens to sea level? → It falls; it recovers when the climate warms again.
6. Era endings: What kind of event ends the Paleozoic and the Mesozoic? → A mass extinction (end-Permian, about 252 million years ago; K–Pg, about 66 million years ago).
7. Climate trend: How has Earth's climate changed since the dinosaurs? → It has cooled, gradually, as the Mesozoic greenhouse faded, ending in repeated ice ages.

blocks.label: B  ·  THE PRECAMBRIAN
items: Eons: Name the three, oldest to youngest: → Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic.
Time: About what share of Earth's history is the Precambrian? → About 88%.
Oldest eon: What sank to form Earth's core? → Dense iron, as the young Earth formed (about 4.54 billion years ago) and separated into layers.
Middle eon: What formed on the surface? What lived there? → Crust and oceans; microbes.

Youngest eon: How did the air change? What caused it? → Oxygen rose (the Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago), because photosynthesis released it faster than rocks and iron could absorb it.
Oxygen: Why did that change matter for life? → It made complex, oxygen-using life possible: eukaryotes, then multicellular life.
Big focus: What was Snowball Earth? About when was it? → Ice reached low latitudes, near the equator: the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations, about 720–635 million years ago (Proterozoic).
The thaw: What ended Snowball Earth? → Volcanoes kept releasing CO₂; it built up until Earth warmed enough to melt the ice.
Bold is the minimum full-credit answer; the rest is detail.

blocks.label: C–E  ·  PERIOD BY PERIOD
rows: Cambrian
Shallow seas; their sand, mud and lime became sandstone, shale and limestone.
Only in the sea.
Warm (greenhouse), with high sea levels; less oxygen than today.
Animal life diversified rapidly into many body plans (trilobites, mollusks, sponges), starting about 539 million years ago.
Ordovician
Mountains; shallow seas still covered large areas.
Reefs and jawless fishes; early land plants.
It cooled; ice grew and sea level fell.
Major extinctions, after the late-Ordovician cooling.
Silurian
Laurentia and Baltica (Caledonian mountain building).
Jawed fishes; small vascular plants and land arthropods built the first land communities.
It warmed, and sea levels recovered.
Devonian
Collisions continued; reefs thrived in warm, shallow seas.
Forests, insects and early tetrapods (four-limbed animals).
Warm and shallow, until late-Devonian crises; extinctions hit hard.
Fish diversified hugely: placoderms, early cartilaginous fish (shark relatives), lobe-finned fish.
Carboniferous
Pangaea, through major collisions (the Appalachians kept growing).
Giant arthropods (Meganeura, Arthropleura) and amphibians.
Oxygen rose above modern levels as CO₂ fell; the tropics stayed warm while southern Gondwana glaciated.
Coal: thick plant material buried in tropical swamps later became coal.
Permian
Pangaea; Panthalassa.
A synapsid, on the mammal line; not a dinosaur.
They warmed and lost oxygen.
Siberian Traps volcanism: greenhouse gases drove warming and ocean oxygen loss; most marine species died, about 252 million years ago.
Triassic
It began rifting apart (late Triassic).
Rebuild, after the end-Permian crisis; reptiles diversified.
Hot, dry and strongly seasonal.
Dinosaurs, about 230 million years ago (not yet dominant).
Jurassic
The Atlantic (and the Gulf of Mexico), as Pangaea split apart.
Giant sauropods (Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus) and theropods (Allosaurus).
Greenhouse (warm); shallow seas covered large areas.
A feathered dinosaur near the origin of birds, about 150 million years ago.
Cretaceous
Forests; high seas flooded broad areas of the continents.
Flowering plants; dinosaurs flourished, and small mammals were present.
High, under greenhouse conditions.
An asteroid impact: a roughly 10 km asteroid hit near the Yucatán (Chicxulub), about 66 million years ago; about 75% of species died, including all non-bird dinosaurs.
Paleogene
India, beginning the Himalaya.
Mammals, into the space left after the K–Pg extinction.
Gradual cooling, as the Mesozoic greenhouse faded.
Neogene
The Himalaya and the Andes.
Grasslands, with grazing mammals.
It got drier (and cooler).
Quaternary
Ice sheets, several kilometers thick.
Humans evolved, during its glacial cycles.
Milankovitch cycles: changes in Earth's orbit and tilt.
The warm interglacial we live in now (the last 11,700 years).
